facts.statement: The study used a deep learning algorithm to identify and separate the lower back muscles from patient-specific CT scans.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: Researchers built two computer simulations: one that included the rib cage and relaxed back muscles, and a control model with only the spine.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The simulations tested how the spine moves when twisting, bending sideways, and bending forward or backward to compare the two models.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The rib cage and relaxed muscles limited twisting movement the most, with much smaller effects on side bending and forward bending.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: When twisting, the upper back became stiffer, but the lower back and waist area actually moved more than in the spine-only model.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: For side bending and forward bending, the presence of the rib cage and muscles reduced movement across all parts of the spine.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The findings suggest that keeping the spine balanced in the front-to-back direction depends mostly on active muscle contraction, not just passive structures.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The study proposes that the rib cage anchors the upper spine, which could force the lower spine to move more to compensate.
facts.subject: computational
